title: System Wall-Clock for Duration Measurement
pattern: Measuring elapsed time, timeouts, or interval durations using `std::time::SystemTime` or system real-time wall-clock timestamps (e.g., subtracting or calling `.elapsed()` on real-time).
why_bad: `SystemTime` (time-of-day clock) is bound to the physical world and is synchronized continuously via Network Time Protocol (NTP) [144, 261]. NTP can adjust, reset, or skew the clock backward or forward at any time, causing elapsed time calculations to yield negative numbers, zero, or excessively large jumps [144, 145]. This can lead to infinite loops, premature timeout triggers, or application crashes [262].
detection: Identify uses of `std::time::SystemTime::now()` or `.elapsed()` on a `SystemTime` instance where the resulting duration is used as a timeout, deadline, rate-limiting bucket window, or loop exit condition.
fix: Use a monotonic clock (e.g., `std::time::Instant::now()`) for measuring elapsed durations, timeouts, or rates, as monotonic clocks are guaranteed to never go backward and are unaffected by NTP wall-clock corrections [144, 251].
source: Martin Kleppmann, *Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, Chapter 8 (Unreliable Clocks) / passages [144, 145, 262]; Brendan Gregg, *Systems Performance*, Clock Drift / passage [9, 261].
